what_it_does: Many scientific and engineering computations require solving large systems of equations where most entries in the matrix are zero — these are called sparse matrices. Solving them efficiently is hard because the irregular pattern of non-zero values causes frequent, unpredictable jumps in memory access. This paper proposes ReSMiPS, a solver that uses Resistive RAM (ReRAM) — a type of memory chip that can also perform analog arithmetic — to do the matrix math directly inside the memory rather than repeatedly shuttling data to a separate processor (a technique called compute-in-memory, or doing math inside the memory chip). To make the analog computation accurate enough for scientific work, the authors invent a new data format called IF64 that achieves the precision of standard 64-bit floating-point numbers in the analog ReRAM arrays, and pair it with a fast algorithm that reorders the sparse matrix entries to improve how cleanly the data maps onto the hardware.
